questions.question: What is the effect of the single setting in "An Inspector Calls"?
questions.correctAnswer: Single setting (dining room) creates claustrophobia - characters cannot physically escape the Inspector. It symbolises their trapped, privileged world. Unity of place intensifies the interrogation and prevents evasion.

questions.question: How does Priestley use dramatic irony with Birling's speeches?
questions.correctAnswer: Birling makes confident predictions ("Titanic is unsinkable", "no war") that 1945 audiences know are false. This undermines his authority, shows capitalist complacency as foolish, and positions audience as superior witnesses.

questions.question: What is real time structure and why does it matter?
questions.correctAnswer: Real time means performance time matches story time. It creates urgency, intensity, and makes audience experience events simultaneously with characters. In "An Inspector Calls", it traps everyone in the moment.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response 30 marks: How does Priestley use dramatic techniques to present the Inspector's power in "An Inspector Calls"? <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Priestley constructs the Inspector as an unstoppable theatrical force through cumulative dramatic techniques that leave the Birlings — and the audience — with no refuge. The lighting shift from "pink and intimate" to "brighter and harder" at his arrival immediately reconfigures the stage from safe domestic space to interrogation room: the audience, like the Birlings, is stripped of comfort and forced into the harsh light of scrutiny. The Inspector's dialogue is Priestley's most precise instrument of power. He controls every exchange through questions — "I'm asking questions" — cutting through Birling's blustering interruptions with short, declarative sentences that demand compliance. When Birling attempts to assert authority by name-dropping "I was an alderman for years," the Inspector simply continues his questioning, theatrically rendering social status irrelevant. On stage, the audience watches the family's hierarchy dissolve as the working-class Inspector commands the room. The real-time structure intensifies this power. With no scene breaks or time jumps, the audience is trapped alongside the characters in an escalating nightmare. The single dining-room set becomes a pressure cooker: characters cannot leave, the Inspector circles them, and each revelation — Gerald's affair, Eric's drinking, Mrs Birling's cruelty — tightens the noose.
